items.stem: Which term matches this description: "West German Chancellor Willy Brandt’s “Eastern policy” of improving relations with the USSR, Poland and the GDR, including the Moscow and Warsaw treaties of 1970"?

items.stem: Leila writes: "The Helsinki Accords were a straightforward victory for the West." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The USSR saw recognition of borders as a major gain; the human rights provisions mattered only gradually as dissidents used them.

items.stem: Noah writes: "Détente ended the Cold War rivalry between the superpowers." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Rivalry continued during détente in the Third World – for example in Angola (1975), the Horn of Africa and Vietnam – and arms competition shifted to MIRVs not covered by SALT I.
items.markingKey: Rivalry continued during détente in the Third World – for example in Angola (1975), the Horn of Africa and Vietnam – and arms competition shifted to MIRVs not covered by SALT I. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Détente was driven more by economic necessity than by a genuine desire for peace." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Economic pressures made détente attractive, but strategic and security considerations were equally important.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI)"?
options: Carter’s statement of January 1980 that the USA would use force to defend its interests in the Persian Gulf
Reagan’s 1983 proposal for a space-based missile defence system, nicknamed “Star Wars”
“restructuring”: Gorbachev’s programme of economic reform, including limited private enterprise (1988 Law on Cooperatives)
The policy of supporting anti-communist insurgencies, such as the mujahideen in Afghanistan and the Contras in Nicaragua
items.answer: Reagan’s 1983 proposal for a space-based missile defence system, nicknamed “Star Wars”
items.markingKey: B. "Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI)" is Reagan’s 1983 proposal for a space-based missile defence system, nicknamed “Star Wars”.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Reagan Doctrine and containment under Truman.
items.answer: Truman’s containment aimed to prevent the spread of communism to new areas; the Reagan Doctrine went further by actively supporting insurgencies to roll back Soviet-backed regimes, such as in Afghanistan, Nicaragua and Angola.
items.markingKey: Truman’s containment aimed to prevent the spread of communism to new areas; the Reagan Doctrine went further by actively supporting insurgencies to roll back Soviet-backed regimes, such as in Afghanistan, Nicaragua and Angola. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Reagan’s policies were the main reason for the end of the Cold War.
items.answer: Reagan’s pressure and diplomacy contributed, but Gorbachev’s choices and Soviet economic weakness were decisive.

items.answer: The Cold War ended through agreements such as the INF Treaty, the fall of Eastern European communism and German reunification (1989–90); the USSR collapsed afterwards in 1991 because of internal economic failure and nationalist movements.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Pan-European Picnic (August 1989) and explain what it reveals about the role of Eastern European states in the collapse of communism.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The economic weakness of the Soviet Union was the main cause of the end of the Cold War."
items.answer: Economic weakness made change necessary, but political decisions determined that the Cold War ended peacefully.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stagnation and falling oil prices after 1985; burden of military spending and Afghanistan; inability to compete with SDI. Arguments against: Gorbachev’s political choices; nationalism in the Baltic states and Eastern Europe; Western diplomacy. Supported judgement: Economic weakness made change necessary, but political decisions determined that the Cold War ended peacefully.

items.stem: "Détente was driven more by economic necessity than by a genuine desire for peace." With reference to specific examples, discuss. [15]
items.answer: Economic pressures made détente attractive, but strategic and security considerations were equally important.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. Indicative content: cost of the arms race and Vietnam for the USA; Soviet need for Western grain and technology; oil shock and inflation in the 1970s; fear of nuclear war after Cuba; European desire for security (Ostpolitik, Helsinki); triangular diplomacy as strategic calculation. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Economic pressures made détente attractive, but strategic and security considerations were equally important. items.stem: In which country did Solidarity win partially free elections in June 1989?
items.answer: Poland
items.markingKey: C. Solidarity won all but one of the contested seats; Tadeusz Mazowiecki became prime minister.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "détente"?
options: The relaxation of tension between the superpowers from the late 1960s to the late 1970s, marked by arms control, trade and summitry
The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of December 1987, which eliminated a whole class of US and Soviet nuclear missiles
“restructuring”: Gorbachev’s programme of economic reform, including limited private enterprise (1988 Law on Cooperatives)
The agreement of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe signed by 35 states in August 1975, recognising post-war borders and committing signatories to human rights
items.answer: The relaxation of tension between the superpowers from the late 1960s to the late 1970s, marked by arms control, trade and summitry
items.markingKey: A. "détente" is the relaxation of tension between the superpowers from the late 1960s to the late 1970s, marked by arms control, trade and summitry.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Reagan Doctrine and containment under Truman.
items.answer: Truman’s containment aimed to prevent the spread of communism to new areas; the Reagan Doctrine went further by actively supporting insurgencies to roll back Soviet-backed regimes, such as in Afghanistan, Nicaragua and Angola.
items.markingKey: Truman’s containment aimed to prevent the spread of communism to new areas; the Reagan Doctrine went further by actively supporting insurgencies to roll back Soviet-backed regimes, such as in Afghanistan, Nicaragua and Angola. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lukas writes: "The revolutions of 1989 were all peaceful." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most were largely peaceful, but in Romania about 1,000 people died and Nicolae Ceaușescu was executed on 25 December 1989.
items.markingKey: Most were largely peaceful, but in Romania about 1,000 people died and Nicolae Ceaușescu was executed on 25 December 1989. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the USSR was interested in détente.
items.answer: Brezhnev wanted recognition of post-war borders in Europe, access to Western technology and grain, a reduction in the cost of the arms race, and to avoid a US–Chinese alliance against it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Brezhnev wanted recognition of post-war borders in Europe, access to Western technology and grain, a reduction in the cost of the arms race, and to avoid a US–Chinese alliance against it. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why Reagan increased US military spending in the early 1980s.
items.answer: Reagan believed the USSR had exploited détente to gain superiority; he wanted to negotiate from strength, restore US confidence after Vietnam and Iran, and pressure the Soviet economy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Reagan believed the USSR had exploited détente to gain superiority; he wanted to negotiate from strength, restore US confidence after Vietnam and Iran, and pressure the Soviet economy. items.stem: "Gorbachev intended to dismantle the Soviet Union." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Gorbachev wanted to reform and preserve socialism and the Union, proposing a new Union Treaty in 1991; collapse was an unintended consequence.

items.stem: "The USSR invaded Afghanistan to gain access to warm-water ports." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Soviet documents show the decision was mainly about saving a failing client regime and fear of losing Afghanistan to US influence or Islamism, not a drive for warm-water ports.
items.markingKey: Soviet documents show the decision was mainly about saving a failing client regime and fear of losing Afghanistan to US influence or Islamism, not a drive for warm-water ports. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source D
The Soviet Union did not lose the Cold War so much as it gave up. Gorbachev’s refusal to use force when Eastern Europe rebelled reflected a change of values, but also a recognition that the empire had become an unaffordable burden.
— Vladislav Zubok, historian, A Failed Empire: The Soviet Union in the Cold War from Stalin to Gorbachev (2007) (paraphrased)

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source D for an historian studying Gorbachev and the end of the Cold War. [4]
items.answer: Value: Zubok uses Soviet archives and interviews with Soviet officials, providing insight into Soviet decision-making. Limitations: It concentrates on Soviet leaders and may underplay Western pressure and popular movements in Eastern Europe.

We seek an open world – open to ideas, open to the exchange of goods and people – a world in which no people, great or small, will live in angry isolation. The era of confrontation is giving way to an era of negotiation.

items.answer: Nixon called for an open world; isolation of any people should end; an era of negotiation was replacing confrontation.
